reasoning: Patient presents with acute altered mental status: delusions of grandiosity (believes he is 'savior of the world'), command hallucinations or disorganized thinking (sent from a location as savior), and dangerous behavior (standing in traffic screaming).

Acute psychiatric decompensation in a young adult with NO prior psychiatric history on file raises concern for organic causes: intoxication, stimulant use, head trauma, infection (meningitis, encephalitis), metabolic derangement, or primary psychotic break.

Patient is refusing assessment and vital signs—this non-compliance, combined with dangerous recent behavior (highway traffic), indicates high risk and inability to self-advocate or cooperate with stabilization.

ESI Decision Point B: Patient meets criteria for ESI-2 (high-risk situation). Acute altered mental status with bizarre/dangerous behavior and unknown etiology is inherently high-risk, regardless of vitals, because life-threatening organic causes (sepsis, intoxication, head injury, electrolyte crisis) must be excluded emergently.

Cannot obtain vital signs at triage; however, absence of vital data in the context of acute delirium/psychosis and dangerous behavior does not reduce acuity—it increases it. Young age does not protect against serious organic pathology.

Differential includes: stimulant intoxication/toxidrome, first-break psychosis (may have medical underpinnings), CNS infection, metabolic encephalopathy, head trauma from traffic, or other acute medical emergency masquerading as pure psychiatric crisis.

Patient should NOT be triaged as ESI-3 or lower given inability to assess risk, refusal of vital signs, acute behavioral danger, and unknown history. Safety principle: err toward higher acuity when organic emergency cannot be ruled out.
red_flags: Acute onset delusions and command/disorganized thinking in patient with no prior psychiatric history
Dangerous behavior: standing in traffic, screaming—indicates severe disorganization and risk to self
Refusal to cooperate with vital signs and assessment—impairs ability to rule out medical emergency
No prior medical or psychiatric record available; cannot exclude organic causes (infection, toxin, trauma, metabolic)
Young age may delay recognition of serious medical illness (clinician bias: 'young = healthy')
First-episode psychosis often has medical etiology in young adults (stimulant use, infection, head injury, autoimmune encephalitis)
Disheveled appearance and police custody suggest possible substance use, homelessness, or acute crisis
